nameStory: Blue grama gets its name from the blue-gray tint of its foliage, especially noticeable when growing in dry conditions. The word 'grama' comes from Spanish 'grama,' meaning grass, reflecting this species' origins in the Spanish-speaking regions of the American Southwest and Mexico.
description: Blue grama is a short, clumping perennial grass that forms dense, low mats rarely growing taller than a foot. This drought-tolerant prairie native has distinctive curved seed heads that look like tiny eyelashes or combs attached to slender stems. The grass blades are narrow and often have a blue-gray or silvery appearance, especially during dry spells. It's a warm-season grass, meaning it does its main growing during the hottest months of summer.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - curved, comb-like seed heads that hang from one side of the stem like tiny eyelashes, usually 2-3 per stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, dense clumps or mats that rarely exceed 12 inches tall, with a bunch-grass appearance rather than spreading runners

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow grass blades with a distinctive blue-gray or silvery-green color, especially when stressed by drought, feeling slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, wiry stems that curve gracefully and feel firm but flexible when bent between your fingers

habitat: In New England, blue grama is extremely rare and typically found only in the driest, most exposed sites with sandy or rocky soils that mimic its native prairie conditions. Look for it in sunny areas like abandoned fields, road cuts, or disturbed ground where most other grasses struggle to survive. It may occasionally appear in xerophytic gardens or naturalized plantings designed to attract native wildlife.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins late in spring as a warm-season grass, appearing as small tufts of blue-green blades emerging from the base of old clumps.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the distinctive curved seed heads appearing in mid to late summer, creating the grass's most recognizable feature.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads mature and turn golden-brown, while the foliage may take on more pronounced blue-gray tones as cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Dormant period with dried, bleached stems and seed heads persisting above ground, creating texture in the winter landscape.

funFact: Blue grama is so perfectly adapted to drought that it can go dormant during dry spells and literally curl up its leaves to reduce water loss, then spring back to life with the next good rainfall - sometimes after months of apparent 'death'!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small bunch grasses, but the curved, comb-like seed heads hanging from one side of the stem are unmistakable. Remember: if it looks like nature's tiny eyelash curler, it's blue grama.
contextualKnowledge: Though blue grama is a keystone species of the Great Plains shortgrass prairie, it's essentially an exotic curiosity in New England's climate. The few observations here likely represent escaped ornamental plantings or accidental introductions rather than established wild populations.
compareHints: Blue grama differs from its relative sideoats grama by having multiple small curved seed heads per stem rather than sideoats' single, larger seed head that dangles conspicuously to one side. Blue grama is also much shorter and more compact, forming tight clumps rather than the more upright, taller growth of sideoats grama.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative blue grama which forms a low carpet and has distinctive eyelash-like flower clusters, sideoats grama grows in upright bunches with its signature one-sided hanging spikes.
